title: Python: tools and approvals
summary: The tools-and-approvals area is the one place a tool runs, and its durable-effect design is strong. A receipt commits under the lease before any effect. A failure is classified as failed or unknown. Readback reconciles interrupted effects. An approval binds the operation identity built from run, instance, tool version and the normalized parsed arguments, and the reviewed hash and resolved target are checked again. The cost of change sits in two functions, `ToolGateway._dispatch` (complexity 19, 15 returns) and `approval_gate` (116 lines, 18 parameters), which took in each new guardrail inline. The approval rule is restated in the catalog, and the approval and receipt state machines are bare strings written from six modules, one of them an adapter. One defect was confirmed by measurement: `search_files` runs a model-supplied regex in a thread, but CPython's `re` holds the GIL, so a catastrophic pattern freezes the worker's event loop, its lease heartbeat and the gateway's own timeout. An approved `browse_goal` call leaves no receipt, so the same call can repeat without a person for up to 24 hours. Key precedence follows the documented order but is coded in four resolvers. Types stop at the database boundary (`Any` connections, rows read by position), and gateway codes are strings matched by hand. `code_tools.search` (61 lines) was read and is acceptable as a pure, tested function. Its only issue is that `truncated` means different things in count mode depending on the target.

scores.why: Project ruff passes on all 13 files and mypy strict is configured, but DH-06 bars are missed: 39 `connection: Any`, 5 blind `except Exception`, 5 narrowing `assert`s, and no enums for approval or receipt states.
tool_gateway.py is a hub: 27 modules import it, adapters use its lease helpers, and it has a cycle with tool_uses. The catalog imports the whole run stack just to list tools.
Most functions are short, but `_dispatch` (19), `approval_gate` (116 lines, 18 parameters) and `browse` (13) concentrate the risky logic, and tool_gateway.py is 594 lines.
Helpers are mostly single-purpose. The cronjob if-chain, re-resolving and re-validating every call, and a GET that writes rows add friction.
13 tool modules sit flat among 41 top-level application files under three naming forms, and tool definitions are split between application/ and adapters/ with no stated rule.

Receipt-before-effect, fencing and readback are well designed. But the regex thread does not bound work, approvals without receipts can be reused, and the catalog rebuilds the worker registry with dummy dependencies.
Most comments explain why and cite decisions and stories. A handful are stale, misplaced or wrong, including one that says a thread bounds a slow regex.
The database boundary is `Any` with rows read by position. Approval and receipt states and gateway codes are bare strings matched by hand, and the decision commands widen contract Literals to `str`.
Typed refusals and the failed/unknown split are careful. Unexpected causes are dropped with no log or receipt detail, and one `suppress(BaseException)` can swallow a cancellation.
The pure parts have focused unit tests and the DB checks cover gateway recovery. Gateway decisions reach unit tests only through a `connection=None` seam, and four risks found here have no test.
The durable-effect design is sound, but central long functions and string-typed state machines make each new guardrail costly to add safely.

strengths.title: One enforcement point that refuses before any effect
strengths.evidence: services/agent/src/autobots/application/tool_gateway.py:1 calls itself the one place a tool runs, and `_dispatch` (322-408) refuses ungranted, unqualified, invalid, out-of-scope or unowned calls before the handler. services/agent/src/autobots/adapters/tool_middleware.py:35-48 answers every SDK tool call from `gateway.execute`. `ToolResult.for_model` (tool_gateway.py:127-135) returns only codes and validated output.

strengths.title: Receipt before effect, fenced, with an explicit failed/unknown split
strengths.evidence: `_effect` (services/agent/src/autobots/application/tool_gateway.py:441-490) commits a 'started' receipt under `hold_running` before the handler runs. `_attempt` (529-554) maps ToolFailed to failed, LeaseLost to denied and anything else to unknown. `_record` (563-594) only moves a receipt forward. `_replay` (492-527) reads back from the destination instead of resending.

strengths.title: Approvals bound to the normalized operation
strengths.evidence: `_operation_id` (services/agent/src/autobots/application/tool_gateway.py:209-213) hashes run, instance, tool, version and the canonical dump of the parsed arguments. `decide` requires the reviewed argument hash and refuses oversized arguments (services/agent/src/autobots/application/approvals.py:273-277). `_target_unchanged` refuses a changed target (tool_gateway.py:216-232). services/agent/tests/test_tools.py:105-133 pins the policy version.

strengths.title: Declarative tool definitions checked at registration and by tests
strengths.evidence: `ToolRegistry.register` (services/agent/src/autobots/application/tool_gateway.py:142-153) refuses unqualified arbitrary execution and retried effects. services/agent/tests/test_tool_catalog.py:35-54 checks that public fields are model fields. services/agent/tests/test_execution_contract.py:23-29 keeps domain/execution.py's TOOL_VERSIONS equal to the registry.

strengths.title: Ports and injected clocks keep browsing testable
strengths.evidence: The browsing loop takes a `Page` Protocol (services/agent/src/autobots/application/browsing_loop.py:59-67), a `Step` callable (142) and a `clock` (226). `browse_tool(None)` describes itself and fails before any container starts (services/agent/src/autobots/application/browsing_tool.py:148-156). services/agent/tests/test_browsing_loop.py:95 opens 12 behavior-named test functions, three of them parametrized, all with fakes.

strengths.title: Secrets never leave key resolution
strengths.evidence: `KeySources` holds markers, never values (services/agent/src/autobots/application/tool_keys.py:146-167). `ToolKeyUnavailable` blocks fallback when a saved secret can't be unsealed (tool_keys.py:69-75, 179-180), as model-gateway.md requires. Key errors name the credential only (61-66).

strengths.title: Why-comments that cite decisions
strengths.evidence: services/agent/src/autobots/application/tool_gateway.py:441-442 says why the receipt commits first, 549 why a success is recorded whoever owns the run, and 571-573 why `_record` only moves forward. services/agent/src/autobots/application/approvals.py:176-183 explains receipt-aware release. services/agent/src/autobots/application/tool_keys.py:1-9 states the precedence order.

strengths.title: Risky paths have behavior-named database checks
strengths.evidence: tests/db/tool_gateway_check.py:163 ('a lost response is reconciled by readback, without repeating') and its check at line 100 ('a stale generation cannot use a tool'), tests/db/effect_check.py and tests/db/approval_check.py:152 ('the next model turn with changed arguments needs its own approval') exercise the gateway and approvals on disposable databases.

findings.title: A model-supplied regex runs under the GIL and can freeze the worker's event loop

locations.note: _search moves search() to a thread, with a comment saying this bounds a slow pattern
re.compile on the model's pattern; each line is matched by pattern.search at 67
pattern: any regular expression up to 200 characters
the only bound is asyncio.wait_for around the handler (10 s for search_files)
the lease heartbeat _keep_lease is a task on the same event loop
DEFAULT_LEASE_SECONDS = 60.0
the worker's status beat shares the loop too

findings.evidence:
async def _search(arguments: SearchFilesInput, context: ToolContext) -> SearchFilesOutput:
    files = await _latest_files(context)
    # In a thread, so the gateway's timeout bounds a slow pattern instead of the event loop.
    return await asyncio.to_thread(search, files, arguments)
CPython's `re` engine holds the GIL for a whole `pattern.search(line)` call. Measured with Python 3.12.16 in a scratch script that touched no project file: `asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.to_thread(...), 0.2)` around `re.compile('(a+)+$').search('a'*25 + 'b')` returned only after 1.90 s, and the event loop ticked once in that time. The same wrapper around `time.sleep(1.9)` returned at 0.20 s with 18 ticks. For this pattern, each added character doubles the time. Run files hold up to 256,000 characters.
findings.impact: One nested-quantifier pattern, written by mistake or steered by third-party text in a run file, stops every task in the worker process. `_keep_lease` can't renew the 60 s lease, the worker's status beat stops, and the 10 s tool timeout can't fire until the match ends. The run is handed to another worker, and the stalled process is fenced only when it wakes. The comment tells maintainers the opposite of what happens.
findings.recommendation: Run `search` where it can be stopped: a child process (stdlib `multiprocessing`, spawn context, with `search` kept in a module with light imports) that is terminated when the tool's time runs out and reported as `ToolFailed('search_timeout')`. This keeps the search pure Python, as Decision 0017 C7 requires. A linear-time engine (`google-re2`) or the `regex` package's `timeout=` would also bound it, but each is a new compiled dependency that needs its own story and a check against C7. Correct the comment. Add a unit test with a pathological pattern that asserts the call ends within the limit while a ticker task keeps running.
findings.sketch:
application/bounded.py
  async def run_in_child(fn, *args, seconds: float) -> T
      # one spawned process; await its result off the loop; terminate() on timeout; raise BoundExceeded
application/code_tools.py
  async def _search(arguments, context):
      files = await _latest_files(context)
      try: return await run_in_child(search, files, arguments, seconds=SEARCH_SECONDS)
      except BoundExceeded: raise ToolFailed('search_timeout') from None
tests/test_code_tools.py
  test_a_catastrophic_pattern_times_out_and_the_loop_keeps_running
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06: keep blocking work off the async event loop and bound timeouts. SP-012: leases must keep renewing. Decision 0017 C7 (search is pure Python, with no rg binary) holds with the stdlib child process. A compiled regex engine would be a new dependency under the delivery rule (story-scoped, pinned and recorded) and would need checking against C7.
findings.verifierNote: Re-measured inline under python3.12 -I with no file written: wait_for(to_thread(...), 0.2) raised TimeoutError only after 1.90 s while a 0.1 s ticker stalled, against 0.20 s for time.sleep(1.9); a to_thread worker also can't be cancelled, so it keeps scanning lines after the timeout. Added Decision 0017 C7 to the recommendation and rule check.

findings.title: `ToolGateway._dispatch` holds every guardrail in one 87-line function and recomputes the call's identity

locations.note: _dispatch: complexity 19, 15 returns, 18 branches (ruff)
50-line inline approval block: condition, target, review detail, gate, target recheck
_operation_id(scope, tool, parsed) at 355, 364, 379 and 396, again at 439; _hash(parsed) also at 383 and 438
metered test written inline, while tool_uses.is_metered (tool_uses.py:186) has no caller
begin_use (71 lines) looks the tool up and validates the arguments again (97-104)
complete_use (7 parameters) looks the tool up a third time (204-205)
`if connection is None: return None`, a seam for unit tests
unit tests reach the pure checks through execute(None, ...)

findings.evidence:
reviewing = ToolContext(connection, scope, _operation_id(scope, tool, parsed))
...
if tool.review_detail is not None and not await _has_approval(
    connection, _operation_id(scope, tool, parsed)
...
    operation_id=_operation_id(scope, tool, parsed),
The guards run in a fixed order (grant, registry, qualification, validation, path grants, ownership, Expert-only, approval, metered budget), each ending in `return _denied(...)`. The field comments cite Decision 0025 V7, Decision 0026 C3 and PRD-Studio GH-06 for parts of the inline approval block.
findings.impact: This is the single enforcement point for every tool call, so each new rule lands in the riskiest function. A reader must confirm by eye that five identity computations agree, and that agreement is what binds an approval to its effect. Unit tests reach the pure checks only by passing `connection=None` and relying on those checks running first. Reordering the guards would crash those tests instead of failing them.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the call once into a frozen `Call` (tool, parsed arguments, argument hash, operation ID), then run named steps. The pure `resolve` step covers grant, registry, qualification, validation and path grants, is tested directly, and replaces the `connection is None` seams. Pass the `Call` to `begin_use`, `complete_use`, `_effect` and `_read` so each call is looked up and validated once. Keep the guard order, the codes and `APPROVAL_POLICY_VERSION` unchanged. Prove behavior with the existing `db` checks (tool_gateway_check, approval_check, effect_check).
findings.sketch:
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Call:  # built once per dispatch
    tool: ToolDefinition; parsed: BaseModel; argument_hash: str; operation_id: str
def resolve(registry, scope, name, arguments) -> Call | ToolResult        # pure, unit-tested
async def admission_refusal(conn, scope, call) -> str | None              # ownership, expert-only
async def hold_for_approval(conn, scope, call) -> str | None              # target, review detail, gate, recheck
async def admit_budget(conn, scope, call, use) -> str | None              # metered calls
async def _dispatch(...): resolve -> admission -> approval if needed -> budget -> _effect | _read
findings.ruleCheck: SP-013: completed arguments are validated before any effect; the sketch keeps validation, ownership, approval and budget in their current order. Decision 0015: no rule or reason text changes, so the policy version stays.
findings.verifierNote: Ruff reports C901 19, PLR0911 15 and PLR0912 18 at tool_gateway.py:322; _operation_id is called at 355, 364, 379, 396 and 439, is_metered has no caller, and five unit tests call execute(None, ...).

findings.title: Approval and receipt states are bare strings changed from six modules, one of them an adapter

locations.note: receipt inserted as 'started'; reopened at 472; moved by _record at 583 and 590
_record: six positional parameters and two near-identical UPDATEs
an operator's ruling sets 'succeeded' or 'failed'
worker loss sets 'unknown'
a stale approval goes back to 'pending'; 'expired' at 208; decided at 299
cancelling sets 'withdrawn'
adapter sends a request back to 'pending' with its own `interval '1 day'` and event, and writes tool_receipts.reconciled_at directly (137-139)
DECIDED is a tuple of strings; no ApprovalStatus or ReceiptStatus enum exists

findings.evidence: rg for 'approval_requests set status|tool_receipts set status|into app_private.tool_receipts' finds 11 statements in tool_gateway.py (4), reconciliation.py, recovery.py, approvals.py (3), runs.py and adapters/github_pulls.py. The values are literals: 'started', 'succeeded', 'failed', 'unknown' and 'pending', 'approved', 'rejected', 'expired', 'withdrawn'. `ToolOutcome` overlaps the receipt values but adds 'denied' and lacks 'started'. The adapter's re-request copies approvals.py:184-199 with a hard-coded day instead of `DEFAULT_TTL_SECONDS`.
findings.impact: No module owns either state machine. A change such as consuming an approval after use (PTOL-06) must reach several modules, including an adapter, and nothing catches a missed writer. The adapter's copy hard-codes the one-day TTL that approvals.py takes from DEFAULT_TTL_SECONDS: the same value today, from a second source. SP-010 asks for these state machines to be documented separately from run status. Today they exist only as scattered SQL.
findings.recommendation: Add `ReceiptStatus` and `ApprovalStatus` StrEnums in the domain, with their permitted transitions and tests. Make a new `application/receipts.py` the only writer of receipt status (start, reopen, record, mark_unknown, rule); `_record` becomes `receipts.record(context, operation_id, outcome)`. Make approvals.py the only writer of approval status (request, return_to_review, expire, decide, withdraw). runs.py, recovery.py, reconciliation.py and the GitHub adapter call these. Document both tables beside SP-010's run table. Stored values stay the same, so no migration is needed. A CHECK constraint, if wanted, is a forward migration.
findings.sketch:
domain/effects.py         ReceiptStatus(StrEnum), ApprovalStatus(StrEnum), RECEIPT_MOVES, APPROVAL_MOVES
application/receipts.py   start / reopen / record / mark_unknown / rule          # sole tool_receipts writer
application/approvals.py  request / return_to_review / expire / decide / withdraw  # sole approval writer
adapters/github_pulls.py  return_to_review -> approvals.return_to_review(conn, operation_id, detail)
runs.apply_command(CANCEL) -> approvals.withdraw_pending(conn, run_id)
tests/test_effect_states.py  every permitted move accepted, every other move refused
findings.ruleCheck: SP-010 (document separate state machines for tool attempts and approvals) and DH-06 (explicit enums; keep tool-attempt and approval states distinct). Values are unchanged and applied migrations are untouched; any constraint is a new forward migration.
findings.verifierNote: Recounted 11 status writes in six modules with the same pattern (github_pulls.py:138 sets only reconciled_at and isn't counted); the adapter's TTL equals DEFAULT_TTL_SECONDS today, so the impact now calls it a second source, not a different value.

findings.title: `approval_gate` takes 18 parameters, three of them optional although Decision 0015 requires them

locations.note: 116 lines, 18 parameters, 9 returns
scope, policy_version and policy_rule default to None
the only caller builds all 16 keyword arguments inline
event plus _enter_wait for a new request
the same event plus wait again for a stale approval
receipt check, repeated in tool_gateway._target_unchanged

findings.evidence: One transaction block locks the request, creates it (reading the requester from the run), decides among pending, approved, rejected and expired, reads the receipt, and reopens a stale approval. The 'approval.requested' event plus `_enter_wait` is written twice. `scope`, `policy_version` and `policy_rule` default to None, though the only caller always passes them.
findings.impact: The optional fields let a future caller store a request without the scope snapshot, policy version and rule that Decision 0015 requires. The decision table (status, expiry, scope match, receipt state) can be exercised only through a database.
findings.recommendation: Pass one frozen `ApprovalProposal` built by the gateway, with the Decision 0015 fields required. Split the body into `_request_review`, `_reopen` and a pure `gate_decision(row, scope_hash, receipt)` that returns release, wait, re-request or a refusal code, and unit-test that table. Share one `_receipt_state` reader with `_target_unchanged`.

async def approval_gate(conn, run: RunRef, proposal, ttl=DEFAULT_TTL_SECONDS) -> str | None

findings.ruleCheck: Decision 0015's fields become required. SP-013's binding (operation identity, argument hash, scope hash, expiry) is unchanged.

findings.title: An approved `browse_goal` call can run again without a person until the approval expires

locations.note: approved, no receipt, not expired: released (return None at 201)
a decision sets expires_at to now plus 24 hours
EFFECTFUL excludes arbitrary_execution, so browse_goal gets no receipt
non-effect calls go to _read, which writes no receipt
approval_required=True; its description (165) says 'A person approves every call.'
operation ID: run, instance, tool, version, argument hash; only workflow steps set instance

findings.evidence: For effects, the receipt makes an approval single-use: a repeated call finds the receipt and replays it. `browse_goal` is `arbitrary_execution`, outside `EFFECTFUL`, so it never gets a receipt. If the model repeats the identical call in the same run, the operation ID is the same, and `approval_gate` finds the request approved, with no receipt and not expired. It returns None, so a second browser session and its paid model calls start with no new approval. Only the metered cap (20 per root run tree) and the run budget limit this. No check in tests/db/browse_goal_check.py repeats an approved call.
findings.impact: Decision 0018 B6 and Decision 0020 L5 require approval on every browse_goal call. Any future read tool that requires approval inherits the same reuse.
findings.recommendation: Consume an approval when it releases a call that leaves no receipt: record `consumed_at` (forward migration) in the releasing transaction, and treat a consumed approval as needing a new request. A crash after release then asks again, which fails safe. Add a db check that repeats an approved browse_goal call and expects approval_pending. Do this inside the approvals owner proposed in PTOL-03.
findings.ruleCheck: Strengthens a guardrail: Decisions 0018 B6 and 0020 L5 (approval on every call) and SP-013 (a replayed approval cannot authorize more work). Any new column is a forward migration.
findings.verifierNote: Traced: browse_goal is arbitrary_execution, so _dispatch sends it to _read with no receipt, and approval_gate's approved branch returns None at 201 for the same operation ID until expiry; no loop-level duplicate-call check exists, and no browse_goal_check case repeats an approved call.

findings.title: tool_gateway.py is a hub: lease fencing and the tool vocabulary live in it, and it has a cycle with tool_uses

locations.note: ownership_refusal, hold_lease, NotRunning, hold_running: run-lease fencing
function-level import of begin_use and complete_use
function-level import of admit_metered
tool_uses imports ToolDefinition, ToolScope, ToolRegistry, ToolResult and hold_lease from the gateway
an adapter imports ownership_refusal from the gateway
another adapter does the same with a local import
the existing lease module, where fencing belongs

findings.evidence: `rg -l 'from autobots.application.tool_gateway import'` lists 27 modules. Eight of them (tools, tool_uses, plans, artifacts, assignments, workflow_runner, adapters/loop_middleware, adapters/browser_executor) import the lease helpers. The gateway needs begin_use, complete_use and admit_metered from tool_uses, which needs the gateway's types, so the gateway imports them inside functions.
findings.impact: Any edit to the gateway invalidates a large share of the package. Adapters reach into the gateway for a lease check, and the cycle forces function-level imports that hide the dependency. The file is 594 lines partly because it holds three concerns.
findings.recommendation: Move ToolScope, ToolContext, ToolDefinition, ToolResult, ToolRegistry, ToolFailed and NotDelivered (lines 20-176) to `application/tool_definitions.py`. Move ownership_refusal, hold_lease, hold_running and NotRunning to `worker_leases.py`. If needed, re-export them from tool_gateway for a short transition, then update importers. tool_gateway then imports tool_uses at the top and keeps dispatch, effects and receipts, under 400 lines.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06: explicit ownership and narrow interfaces. No behavior change, and the DH-03 layer layout is unchanged.
findings.verifierNote: Recounted 27 importing modules in src (14 more in tests); an AST scan finds exactly the eight lease-helper importers named; tool_gateway imports tool_uses only inside execute (310) and _dispatch (402).

findings.evidence: catalog_registry's docstring says it is built as the worker builds it, but the extras (APPROVAL_GATE, browse_tool) are mirrored by hand. test_every_registered_tool_appears_once_and_nothing_else derives both sides from `catalog_registry()`. tool_catalog.py is 348 lines covering registry assembly, JSON-schema walking, guides, descriptors, filtering and grant availability.
findings.impact: A tool added to or removed from a worker's extras can be missing from the catalog, or wrongly listed in it, and no test fails. PRD-Tool-Catalog TC-01 says the catalog derives from the registry the worker runs. The dummy `object()` dependency breaks as soon as a factory touches its dependency at build time.

Follow browse_tool's pattern: with no runtime, a definition still describes itself, and its handler fails before any effect. loop_registry, the workflow runner, the worker, the catalog and test_execution_contract all call it. Add one parity test: the catalog's registered set equals the set a qualified worker builds, workflow extras included.
findings.ruleCheck: PRD-Tool-Catalog TC-01 (the catalog derives from the worker's registry). AB-02 and Decision 0025 V6 are kept: browse_goal is registered only while qualified and switched on, and the switch stays an input.
